books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: John C. Calhoun, speech on the slavery question, read in the Senate by James M. Mason, March 4, 1850

stimulus.source_note: John C. Calhoun, speech on the slavery question, read in the Senate by Senator James M. Mason, March 4, 1850 (Congressional Globe, 31st Congress, 1st session). Public domain.
stimulus.text:
I have, Senators, believed from the first that the agitation of the subject of slavery would, if not prevented by some timely and effective measure, end in disunion.

. . .

You have thus had forced upon you the greatest and the gravest question that can ever come under your consideration: How can the Union be preserved?

. . .

To this question there can be but one answer, — that the immediate cause is the almost universal discontent which pervades all the States composing the Southern section of the Union.

. . .

It is a great mistake to suppose that disunion can be effected by a single blow. The cords which bind these States together in one common Union are far too numerous and powerful for that. Disunion must be the work of time.

. . .

I return to the question with which I commenced, How can the Union be saved? There is but one way by which it can with any certainty; and that is, by a full and final settlement, on the principle of justice, of all the questions at issue between the two sections.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Calhoun's warning that agitation over slavery would “end in disunion” most directly reflects his belief that

options.text: the North and South had already agreed to separate peacefully.
options.misconception: Calhoun warns of disunion as a disaster to prevent, not as a peaceful agreement already made.

options.text: the Union would break apart slowly, as agitation wore away its bonds.
one violent act by abolitionists would destroy the Union overnight.
options.misconception: Calhoun says the opposite: disunion cannot be effected “by a single blow,” but must be “the work of time.”

options.text: the Constitution already gave the South the right to secede at will.
options.misconception: Calhoun never claims a constitutional right to secede in this speech; he asks how the Union can be preserved, not how to leave it.

rationales.A: Calhoun warns of disunion as a disaster to prevent, not as a peaceful agreement already made.
rationales.B: Calhoun says disunion cannot come “by a single blow” because the cords binding the states are too many and powerful; instead, “Disunion must be the work of time.”
rationales.C: Calhoun says the opposite: disunion cannot be effected “by a single blow,” but must be “the work of time.”
rationales.D: Calhoun never claims a constitutional right to secede in this speech; he asks how the Union can be preserved, not how to leave it.
rationales.general:
1. Picture the Union as Calhoun pictures it: cords, many and powerful, binding the states together.
2. Ask what could break cords that strong: not one blow, but years of agitation wearing at them.
3. See why he warns now: if the wearing goes on unchecked, the cords part on their own.
Remember: a slow danger is still a danger; watch for the speaker who warns about time, not just about one event.
